raw_case_text:
The patient, an 81-year-old male Chinese farmer, had a 20-year history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In the past, he had smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes for 37 years but had been a non-smoker for the previous 30 years. Over the previous three years, he had been hospitalized at our facility for acute exacerbations of COPD (AECOPD), averaging 1-3 hospitalizations per year. The patient had been on a regimen of salmeterol fluticasone 50 mug/500 muG, 1 inhalation twice daily, and tiotropium bromide inhalation once daily for an extended period, with his symptoms remaining manageable.
The patient had experienced cough, expectoration, chest tightness, and shortness of breath for about four days before admission but reported no chills, fever, chest pain, or hemoptysis. He had received anti-infection treatment at a local clinic (specifics of the diagnosis and treatment are unknown), but after four days of medication, his symptoms showed minimal improvement, leading to his admission to our hospital.
There was no evidence of fever during his hospitalization. Lung auscultation revealed scattered wet rales, and there was mild edema in both lower extremities. Laboratory results (detailed in Table 1) included a blood gas analysis indicating an oxygenation index of 372 mmHg. Blood tests showed elevated white blood cell (WBC) and neutrophil counts (11.6*10^9/L), with an absolute lymphocyte value of 0.3*10^9/L and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 123.11 mg/L. Blood biochemistry highlighted hypoproteinemia (25.9 g/L), IgE at 209.4 IU/mL, and reduced cortisol levels. Chest computed tomography (CT) scan shows a small amount of pleural effusion on both sides (Figure 1), multiple nodules in the upper lobe of the left lung (Figure 1A and B), and the middle lobe of the right lung (Figure 1C).  
The patient received successive piperacillin tazobactam, fluconazole, and methylprednisolone injections but his cough and expectoration persisted. His condition improved after switching to oral itraconazole capsules for fungal treatment, leading to his discharge. However, three days after discharge, he presented with bloody sputum, worsened chest tightness, shortness of breath, and left chest and rib pain, necessitating readmission.
His body temperature was normal on admission, with scattered dry and wet rales audible in both lungs. Laboratory tests revealed a reduced oxygenation index (248 mmHg), elevated WBC and neutrophil counts (20.9*10^9/L), a reduced lymphocyte count (0.2*10^9/l), a CRP level of 198.3 mg/L, a procalcitonin (PCT) level of 1.74 ng/mL, and hypoproteinemia (22.3 g/l). He was then treated with cefoperazone sulbactam and voriconazole injections.
Four weeks later, enhanced chest CT scans indicated worsening of the lung lesions and a significant increase in the pleural effusion in the left lung (Figure 2), together with multiple patchy high-density shadows in both lungs (Figure 2) and partial cavity formation (Figure 2A-C). A thoracic drain was placed in the patient, yielding a purulent reddish-brown fluid (Figure 3), later confirmed as empyema. Sputum cultures isolated Pseudomonas aeruginosa.  
The patient's condition deteriorated over the next few days, with increased chest tightness, shortness of breath, and fatigue. Despite the addition of methylprednisolone and meropenem, together with noninvasive ventilator support, his condition continued to decline. The laboratory results indicated further deterioration, with a reduced oxygenation index (166 mmHg), worsening blood counts, and signs of multi-organ dysfunction. Gram staining of sputum smears showed positive bacilli (Figure 4A) and acid-fast-bacterial staining showed weak positivity (Figure 4B), Finally, after culture on Columbia blood agar medium, the VITEK test   and mass spectrometry identified the Nocardia otitidiscaviarum (Figure 4C). The pleural fluid also tested positive for N. otitidiscaviarum. The patient was thus diagnosed with severe N. otitidiscaviarum infection and sepsis, and was treated with linezolid, ciprofloxacin, Sulfamethoxazole, and nutritional support. Despite these measures, his condition deteriorated rapidly. 
Three days later, the patient's dyspnea had worsened, and a bedside chest X-ray revealed a left hydropneumothorax, compressing approximately 30% of the left lung. He was transferred to the ICU suffering from multiple organ failure, including respiratory, cardiac, hepatic, and renal failure, together with disseminated intravascular coagulation, septic shock, and secondary thrombocytopenia. Despite aggressive treatments including mechanical ventilation, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), fluid resuscitation, and multiple drug therapies, the patient, unfortunately, succumbed to the illness two weeks after diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 81-year-old male Chinese farmer with severe COPD presented with a 4-day history of cough, expectoration, chest tightness, and dyspnea, followed by readmission 3 days after discharge for hemoptysis, worsening dyspnea, and left pleuritic chest pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with 4 days of cough, expectoration, chest tightness, and shortness of breath unresponsive to clinic antibiotics. He was treated with piperacillin-tazobactam, fluconazole, methylprednisolone, and oral itraconazole and discharged, but was readmitted 3 days later with bloody sputum, worsening chest tightness, dyspnea, and left chest/rib pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: 20-year history of COPD with 1-3 hospitalizations per year over the prior 3 years for acute exacerbations, maintained on inhaled salmeterol/fluticasone (50/500 ug twice daily) and tiotropium bromide (once daily). Former smoker (1.5 packs/day for 37 years, quit 30 years prior); Chinese farmer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for chills, fever, chest pain, or hemoptysis on first admission; positive for bloody sputum and left chest/rib pain on readmission.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile on both admissions. Initial exam showed scattered wet rales in the lungs and mild bilateral lower extremity edema. Readmission exam showed scattered bilateral dry and wet rales.
objective.routine_investigations: First admission labs: oxygenation index (PaO2/FiO2) 372 mmHg, WBC 11.6 x 10^9/L, absolute lymphocytes 0.3 x 10^9/L, CRP 123.11 mg/L, hypoproteinemia (25.9 g/L), IgE 209.4 IU/mL, and reduced serum cortisol. Readmission labs: oxygenation index 248 mmHg (later dropping to 166 mmHg), WBC 20.9 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.2 x 10^9/L, CRP 198.3 mg/L, procalcitonin 1.74 ng/mL, and total protein 22.3 g/L. Bedside chest X-ray later showed a left hydropneumothorax compressing ~30% of the left lung.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial chest CT showed small bilateral pleural effusions and multiple nodules in the left upper lobe and right middle lobe. Repeat enhanced chest CT 4 weeks after readmission showed marked progression with a large left pleural effusion, bilateral patchy consolidations, and partial cavitation. Thoracic drainage yielded reddish-brown purulent empyema fluid.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Severe pleuropulmonary nocardiosis (cavitary pneumonia, left empyema, and hydropneumothorax) and sepsis caused by Nocardia otitidiscaviarum (with Pseudomonas aeruginosa co-infection in sputum) was confirmed: sputum smears showed Gram-positive, weakly acid-fast bacilli, and both sputum and pleural fluid cultures on Columbia blood agar grew Nocardia otitidiscaviarum identified by VITEK mass spectrometry. Despite switching from empirical cefoperazone-sulbactam, voriconazole, meropenem, and methylprednisolone to targeted therapy with linezolid, ciprofloxacin, and sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), alongside chest tube drainage, mechanical ventilation, and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) for multiorgan failure, septic shock, and DIC, the patient died 2 weeks after diagnosis.
